svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Bulk transport: the cell membrane folds to take materials in (endocytosis) or out (exocytosis). All need ATP."], [1, "Phagocytosis: pseudopodia surround a large particle."], [4, "Pinocytosis: small droplets of fluid are taken in."], [7, "Receptor-mediated: specific molecules bind receptors in a coated pit, which pinches off."], [11, "Exocytosis: a vesicle fuses with the membrane and releases its contents."]]
svg.title: Endocytosis and exocytosis
svg.desc: Four panels: phagocytosis with pseudopodia engulfing a bacterium, pinocytosis forming small fluid vesicles, receptor-mediated endocytosis with ligands binding receptors in a clathrin-coated pit, and exocytosis of a vesicle.
svg.text: Membrane in orange; outside the cell is at the top of each panel.

g.data-info: Large particles such as bacteria are engulfed by pseudopodia and enclosed in a phagosome. By phagocytes and some protists.
The membrane folds in around droplets of extracellular fluid and whatever is dissolved in it, forming small vesicles. Not specific.

Specific molecules (e.g. LDL carrying cholesterol) bind receptors gathered in pits coated with the protein clathrin; the pit pinches off as a coated vesicle. Very specific and concentrates the molecule.
The reverse: vesicles from the Golgi fuse with the cell surface membrane and release their contents, e.g. hormones, enzymes, neurotransmitters.
All four rely on the fluid phospholipid bilayer, which can bend, pinch off and fuse; they use ATP (active processes).
